title: Dependency Injection in Functions
description: Use dependency injection in isolated-process Azure Functions to keep function code clean and testable.

data.text: The isolated worker model uses the standard Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection container. This means you can register services the same way you do in ASP.NET Core — with AddSingleton, AddScoped, or AddTransient — and inject them into your function classes.

Because Functions are stateless, Singleton and Transient are the most common lifetimes. Scoped services are only useful when you explicitly create a scope (for example, per-request in an HTTP function).

cards.title: Singleton
cards.description: One instance per Functions host process. Good for caches, HTTP clients, and read-only config.
cons: State persists for the life of the host

cards.title: Transient
cards.description: A new instance every time it is requested. Good for lightweight stateless services.

cards.title: Scoped
cards.description: One instance per explicit scope. Use with CreateScope() inside an HTTP function.

data.text: Using Scoped Services in HTTP Functions
When you inject a DbContext or similar scoped service, create a scope at the top of your HTTP function using the IServiceProvider that the runtime provides.

data.text: Because functions are plain classes with constructor-injected dependencies, you can test them with any test framework — no Azure runtime needed.

data.title: WeatherFunctionTests.cs — unit test with mocked dependencies
Keep functions thin
data.text: Put all business logic in separate services injected via DI. Functions should only handle trigger orchestration and response building. This makes your code testable and reusable outside Azure.

data.title: Refactor a function to use injected services
data.description: Take a function that has inline data access logic and refactor it to use DI.
steps: Create an IReportService interface with a GenerateCsvAsync method
Refactor the function method to inject IReportService instead of building the CSV inline
Write a unit test that mocks IReportService and verifies the HTTP response
data.expectedOutcome: The function body is under 15 lines and delegates all business logic to the injected service.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Prefer Singleton for caches and HTTP clients; create scopes manually for DbContext
Keep functions thin — inject services and test them in isolation
Use IHttpClientFactory for outbound HTTP instead of new HttpClient()
data.takeaway: DI in Azure Functions follows the same patterns as ASP.NET Core, so your existing service architecture transfers directly.
